name: Marcel waving

lead: Marcel waving, or marcelling, uses heated curling tongs to press deep, uniform waves into straight hair. The payoff is a sleek, sculpted wave associated with 1920s glamour.
It is credited to French hairdresser Marcel Grateau in the 1870s and peaked in the 1920s and 1930s, often with bobbed hair.

paras: A stylist or user works the heated tongs through sections of dry hair, then lets the waves cool in place. Modern vintage styling uses adjustable-temperature irons.
Heat styling can scorch or dry hair, and early irons risked burns. Heat protection and temperature control are standard advice from stylists.

angle.text: The method gives straight hair a defined wave pattern for a vintage look, especially on short or bobbed cuts.

lead: Marcel waving, also called marcelling, is a hair-styling technique that sets a regular wave using hot curling tongs. It produces a deep, sculpted wave similar in look to a finger wave but made with heat.[1]

French hairdresser Marcel Grateau (1852-1936) is widely credited with inventing it in the 1870s, with sources giving 1872 or 1875.[1] He took the name François Marcel Woelfflé in the United States, where patents were filed in 1905 for a curling iron and in 1918 for an electric hair-waving iron.[1] The style was popular in the 1920s with bobs and is associated with wearers such as Josephine Baker.[1] Grokipedia adds that Grateau opened a Montmartre salon in 1872 and that electric irons followed in the 1920s.[2]

paras: The technique uses heated, rounded tongs to bend sections of hair into alternating S-curves, the style concentrating waves on the top and sides.[1][2] It differs from finger waving, which is formed on wet hair by hand and comb.[2]

Grateau is credited with the technique in the 1870s.[1] A 1905 patent covered a curling iron and a 1918 patent an electric hair-waving iron.[1] The style peaked in the 1920s, and it appears in songs, the name of the doo-wop group The Marcels and the film Some Like It Hot.[1]
Early practitioners tested iron heat on paper to avoid scorching hair, and electric irons with temperature control later reduced the risk.[2]
